beats.text: GPS satellites have no idea where you are. Your phone does all the work.
Around thirty GPS satellites circle Earth, about twenty thousand kilometres up.
beats.dir: calm, factual, a sense of scale

beats.text: They don't track you. They just broadcast two things, nonstop: where they are, and exactly what time it is.
Your phone listens. Even at light speed, each signal takes a tiny fraction of a second to arrive.
Multiply that delay by the speed of light, and you get your distance from that satellite.
One satellite puts you on a giant sphere. Three narrow it to one point. A fourth fixes your phone's clock.
The timing is so precise that Einstein matters: up there, satellite clocks run about thirty-eight microseconds a day fast.
Ignore that, and your location would drift by more than eleven kilometres in a single day.
So when your map finds you instantly, remember: the satellites are just clocks. The genius is in your pocket.
